Pathology.question: ১) Most common tumor of the salivary gland
Pathology.exp:
Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) is the most common salivary gland tumor, accounting for approximately 60–70% of all salivary gland neoplasms. It most commonly arises in the parotid gland and is benign, although it has a risk of malignant transformation if longstanding.

High-Yield

Category Most Common Tumor
Overall salivary gland tumor Pleomorphic adenoma
Most common benign Pleomorphic adenoma
Most common malignant Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Second most common benign parotid tumor Warthin tumour

Rapid Recall

  • Pleomorphic adenoma = Most common salivary gland tumor

  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma = Most common malignant salivary gland tumor

  • Warthin tumour = Smoking-associated, almost exclusively parotid

Pathology.question: ২) Which type of emphysema is seen in α1-antitrypsin deficiency
Pathology.exp:
α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar (panlobular) emphysema, in which the entire acinus (from respiratory bronchiole to alveoli) is uniformly destroyed. It predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lungs.

High-Yield

Type of Emphysema Association Predominant Site
Panacinar (Panlobular) α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency Lower lobes
Centriacinar (Centrilobular) Smoking Upper lobes
Distal acinar (Paraseptal) Spontaneous pneumothorax Peripheral lung
Irregular Scarring/Fibrosis Variable

Rapid Recall

  • α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency → Panacinar emphysema → Lower lobes

  • Smoking → Centriacinar emphysema → Upper lobes

Pathology.question: ৩) Common complication of pneumonia
Pathology.exp:
The most common complication of pneumonia is parapneumonic pleural effusion, which is a pleural effusion associated with pneumonia. It may be:

  • Uncomplicated (sterile exudate)

  • Complicated (infected)

  • Progress to empyema if pus accumulates in the pleural space.

High-Yield

Complication Frequency
Parapneumonic effusion Most common
Empyema Common severe pleural complication
Lung abscess Seen with aspiration or necrotizing infection
ARDS Severe, uncommon
Pneumothorax Rare

Rapid Recall

  • Most common complication of pneumonia → Parapneumonic effusion

  • Most common pleural complication → Parapneumonic effusion

  • Empyema = Infected pleural fluid (pus)

Pathology.question: ৪) Bronchiectasis usually affects
Pathology.exp:
Bronchiectasis most commonly involves the lower lobes of both lungs, particularly in post-infectious and idiopathic disease. Chronic infection and impaired mucociliary clearance lead to permanent bronchial dilatation, which is most often bilateral and lower lobe predominant.

High-Yield

Condition Typical Distribution
Bronchiectasis (usual) Bilateral lower lobes
Cystic fibrosis Bilateral upper lobes
Post-TB bronchiectasis Upper lobes
Obstructing tumor/foreign body Localized unilateral bronchiectasis

Rapid Recall

  • Typical bronchiectasis → Bilateral lower lobes

  • Upper lobe bronchiectasis → Think cystic fibrosis or previous tuberculosis

  • Localized unilateral bronchiectasis → Think bronchial obstruction

Pathology.question: ৫) Most common site of carcinoid tumor-
Pathology.exp:
In classical pathology and MBBS/FCPS examinations, the vermiform appendix is considered the most common site of gastrointestinal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors. These tumors are often small, incidental findings during appendicectomy, and usually have an excellent prognosis.

High-Yield

Site Key Point
Appendix Most common site (classic exam answer)
Terminal ileum Most common site associated with carcinoid syndrome and metastatic disease
Rectum Third common GI site
Stomach Less common

Rapid Recall

  • Most common site (FCPS/MBBS) → Appendix

  • Carcinoid syndrome → Usually terminal ileal tumors with liver metastasis

  • Neuroendocrine tumor marker → Chromogranin A

Pathology.question: ৬) Most common cause of cirrhosis of liver -
Pathology.exp:
Among the given options, alcoholic liver disease is the most common cause of cirrhosis in classical pathology and physiology examinations.

Raid Recall

  • Classic FCPS/MBBS answer: Alcoholic cirrhosis

  • Post-necrotic cirrhosis: Often follows viral hepatitis

  • Cryptogenic cirrhosis: Frequently due to unrecognized MASLD/NASH in modern practice

Pathology.question: ৭) Focal cerebral infarcts are most commonly
৮) Stages of lobar pneumonia excludes
Pathology.exp:
The classical stages of lobar pneumonia are:

  1. Congestion (0–24 hours)

  2. Red hepatization (1–3 days)

  3. Gray hepatization (3–8 days)

  4. Resolution (after ~8 days)

There is no stage called "blue hepatization."

Rapid Recall

Lobar pneumonia stages:

  1. Congestion

  2. Red hepatization

  3. Gray hepatization

  4. Resolution

Mnemonic: C → R → G → R (Congestion → Red → Gray → Resolution)

Pathology.question: ৯) HTN with radiofemoral delay indicates
Pathology.exp:
Radiofemoral delay is a classic clinical sign of coarctation of the aorta. The narrowing of the aorta (usually just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery) delays blood flow to the lower limbs.

Clinical features:

  • Hypertension in the upper limbs

  • Low blood pressure in the lower limbs

  • Delayed or weak femoral pulses compared with radial pulses (radiofemoral delay)

  • Systolic murmur over the back/interscapular region

Rapid Recall

  • Radiofemoral delay = Coarctation of the aorta

  • Upper limb BP > Lower limb BP

  • Rib notching on chest X-ray due to collateral intercostal arteries

  • Associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve

Pathology.question: ১০) Which organism is found in pneumonia after organ transplant recipient?
Pathology.exp:
Legionella pneumophila is a well-recognized cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, particularly solid organ transplant recipients and those receiving immunosuppressive therapy

Rapid Recall

  • Organ transplant → Legionella

  • Legionella diagnosis: Urinary antigen (especially serogroup 1)

  • Treatment: Azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (e.g., levofloxacin)

Pathology.question: ১১) Most frequent presentation of RPGN
Pathology.exp:
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome characterized by a rapid decline in renal function with crescent formation on renal biopsy.

Among the given options, post-infectious glomerulonephritis is the most frequent underlying disease associated with RPGN.

High-Yield

Causes of RPGN:

  • Type I (Anti-GBM): Goodpasture syndrome

  • Type II (Immune complex): Post-infectious GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis

  • Type III (Pauci-immune): ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA)

Rapid Recall

  • Most common underlying disease (among these options): Post-infectious GN

  • Classic anti-GBM disease: Goodpasture syndrome

  • Minimal change disease → Nephrotic syndrome, not RPGN

  • Hallmark of RPGN: Crescentic glomerulonephritis

Pathology.question: ১২) Features of irreversible cell injury-
Pathology.exp:
Among the given options, lysosomal swelling is the best answer representing irreversible cell injury, as it progresses to lysosomal membrane rupture with release of hydrolytic enzymes, leading to autodigestion and necrosis.

High-Yield

Reversible cell injury

  • Cellular swelling (hydropic change)

  • Fatty change

  • Loss of microvilli

  • Membrane blebbing

  • Mitochondrial swelling

  • ER dilatation

  • Chromatin clumping

Irreversible cell injury

  • Severe membrane damage

  • Lysosomal membrane rupture

  • Massive Ca²⁺ influx

  • Nuclear changes: Pyknosis → Karyorrhexis → Karyolysis

Rapid Recall

  • Reversible: Cell swelling, loss of microvilli, chromatin clumping

  • Irreversible: Lysosomal rupture, membrane disruption, nuclear breakdown (pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis)

Pathology.question: ১৩) Cardiac output high, base deficit high and venous pressure low. Which type of shock is related to it-
Pathology.exp:
The hemodynamic profile described is characteristic of early distributive (especially septic) shock:

  • High cardiac output ✔ (due to marked peripheral vasodilation)

  • High base deficit ✔ (reflects lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion)

  • Low venous pressure (CVP) ✔ (due to venodilation and relative hypovolemia)

Rapid Recall

  • High CO + Low CVP + Low SVR = Distributive shock

  • Base deficit is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion and lactic acidosis.

  • In late septic shock, cardiac output may eventually fall.

Pathology.question: ১৪) Phlebothrombosis differs from thrombophlebitis-
Pathology.option1: It is thrombosis of inflamed vein
Pathology.option2: It mainly occurs in small artery
Pathology.option3: It is usually small in size
Pathology.option4: It may occur at any vein
Pathology.exp:
Phlebothrombosis is venous thrombosis without significant inflammation of the vein wall, whereas thrombophlebitis is thrombosis associated with inflammation.

The key difference is that phlebothrombosis can occur in both superficial and deep veins (i.e., essentially any vein), while thrombophlebitis most commonly affects superficial veins.

Rapid Recall

  • Phlebothrombosis = Thrombus first, inflammation later (or absent).

  • Thrombophlebitis = Inflammation first, then thrombus.

  • DVT is a form of phlebothrombosis and has a higher risk of pulmonary

Pathology.question: ১৫) Cumulative sub lethal injury over long life span causes
১৬) Which one is double edged sword?
Pathology.exp:
Metaplasia is considered a "double-edged sword" because it is initially a protective adaptive response, but persistent stimulation can lead to dysplasia and eventually malignancy.

Examples:

  • Smoking: Normal ciliated columnar epithelium → Stratified squamous metaplasia, increasing the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Barrett oesophagus: Squamous epithelium → Intestinal columnar metaplasia, increasing the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

High-Yield

  • Metaplasia = Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another mature cell type.

  • Persistent stimulus → Dysplasia → Carcinoma.

Rapid Recall

  • Double-edged sword in cellular adaptation = Metaplasia

  • Protective initially, but prolonged injury increases cancer risk

  • Mnemonic: Metaplasia → Malignancy risk.

Pathology.question: ১৭) Ischemic necrosis of brain indicates which type of necrosis?
Pathology.exp:
Ischemic infarction of the brain characteristically causes liquefactive necrosis because the brain has a high content of lipids and hydrolytic enzymes, leading to enzymatic digestion of dead tissue.

In contrast, ischemic infarction of all other solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen) typically produces coagulative necrosis.

Rapid Recall

  • Brain infarction → Liquefactive necrosis

  • All other ischemic infarcts → Coagulative necrosis

  • TB → Caseous necrosis

  • Pancreatitis → Fat necrosis

Pathology.question: ১৮) CA-125 is a tumour marker for
Pathology.exp:
CA-125 (Cancer Antigen 125) is the most widely used tumor marker for epithelial ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

It is mainly used for:

  • Monitoring response to treatment

  • Detecting recurrence

  • Supporting diagnosis in women with an adnexal mass (it is not suitable as a screening test because it lacks specificity).

Rapid Recall

  • CA-125 → Ovary

  • CA 19-9 → Pancreas

  • AFP → Liver

  • PSA → Prostate

  • CEA → Colon (monitoring)

Pathology.question: ১৯) Grading of cancer is based on
Pathology.exp:
Tumor grading assesses the degree of differentiation of tumor cells and reflects how closely they resemble the normal tissue from which they arise. It provides an indication of the tumor's biological aggressiveness.

  • Well-differentiated (Grade I) → Resembles normal tissue, better prognosis.

  • Moderately differentiated (Grade II)

  • Poorly differentiated (Grade III)

  • Undifferentiated/Anaplastic (Grade IV) → Highly aggressive, poor prognosis

    Rapid Recall

    • Grade = Differentiation

    • Stage = TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis)

    Mnemonic:
    G = Grade = Gland-like (Differentiation)
    S = Stage = Spread (TNM)

Pathology.question: ২০) Human papilloma virus is responsible for
Pathology.exp:
Human papillomavirus (HPV), especially high-risk types 16 and 18, is the principal etiological agent for carcinoma of the cervix. HPV oncogenes E6 and E7 inactivate the tumor suppressor proteins p53 and Rb, promoting malignant transformation.

Rapid Recall

  • HPV → Cervical carcinoma

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma

  • HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma

  • Merkel cell polyomavirus → Merkel cell carcinoma

Pathology.question: ২১) Protooncogene is converted to oncogene by
Pathology.exp:
A proto-oncogene is a normal gene involved in regulating cell growth. It can be converted into an oncogene by several genetic mechanisms, including:

  • Point mutation

  • Gene amplification

  • Chromosomal translocation ✔

  • Insertional mutagenesis (viral)

Among the given options, chromosomal translocation is the best answer, as it is a classic mechanism of proto-oncogene activation in human cancers.

Examples:

  • t(8;14) → c-MYC activation in Burkitt lymphoma

  • t(9;22) → BCR-ABL fusion in Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)

High-Yield

Proto-oncogene → Oncogene

  • Point mutation (e.g., RAS)

  • Gene amplification (e.g., HER2/neu, N-MYC)

  • Chromosomal translocation (e.g., c-MYC, BCR-ABL)

Rapid Recall

  • Burkitt lymphoma: t(8;14) → c-MYC

  • CML: t(9;22) → BCR-ABL

  • HER2: Gene amplification

  • RAS: Point mutation

Pathology.question: ২২) Angiogenesis is promoted by
Pathology.exp:
Angiogenesis is promoted by several growth factors, including:

  • VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor) – most important

  • FGF (Fibroblast Growth Factor)

  • PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor) – promotes recruitment of pericytes and smooth muscle cells, helping maturation and stabilization of newly formed vessels.

High-Yield

Promoters of angiogenesis

  • VEGF (most important)

  • FGF

  • PDGF

  • TGF-β

  • Angiopoietins

Inhibitors of angiogenesis

  • Endostatin

  • Thrombospondin

  • Angiostatin

Rapid Recall

  • VEGF = Initiates new vessel formation

  • PDGF = Matures and stabilizes new vessels

  • Endostatin & Thrombospondin = Inhibit angiogenesis

  • Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α) increases VEGF expression in hypoxic tissues.

Pathology.question: ২৩) Anesthetic accident produces
Pathology.exp:
An anesthetic accident (especially due to spinal or epidural anesthesia causing sympathetic blockade) classically produces neurogenic shock.

Mechanism:

  • Loss of sympathetic tone

  • Peripheral vasodilation

  • Hypotension

  • Bradycardia (due to unopposed vagal activity)

  • Warm, dry skin

Rapid Recall

  • Spinal anesthesia → Neurogenic shock

  • Hypotension + Bradycardia + Warm skin = Neurogenic shock

  • Sympathetic blockade is the underlying mechanism.

Pathology.question: ২৪) Cause of redness in acute inflammation is-
Pathology.exp:
The redness (rubor) of acute inflammation is caused by arteriolar vasodilation, which leads to increased blood flow (hyperemia) to the affected tissue. This vasodilation is mainly mediated by histamine and nitric oxide.

Rapid Recall

  • Rubor + Calor → Vasodilation → Increased blood flow

  • Tumor → Increased vascular permeability

  • Dolor → Bradykinin + PGE₂

  • Stasis → Leukocyte margination

Pathology.question: ২৫) Emigration of leukocyte to the site of injury is called-
Pathology.exp:
Diapedesis (transmigration) is the process by which leukocytes pass through the endothelial cell junctions of postcapillary venules to leave the bloodstream and enter the site of tissue injury.

Sequence of leukocyte recruitment:

  1. Margination

  2. Rolling (Selectins)

  3. Firm adhesion (Integrins)

  4. Diapedesis (Transmigration) ✔

  5. Chemotaxis (Movement toward the site of injury)

Key molecules

  • Rolling: Selectins

  • Adhesion: Integrins (ICAM-1, VCAM-1)

  • Diapedesis: PECAM-1 (CD31)

Rapid Recall

  • Rolling = Selectins

  • Adhesion = Integrins

  • Diapedesis = PECAM-1 (CD31)

  • Chemotaxis = C5a, IL-8, LTB₄, bacterial products

Pathology.question: ২৬) Accumulation of cholesterol occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Xanthomas are localized accumulations of cholesterol-rich lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in the skin, tendons, or subcutaneous tissues. They are commonly associated with hypercholesterolemia and other disorders of lipid metabolism.

Rapid Recall

  • Xanthoma → Cholesterol

  • Anthracosis → Carbon

  • Asbestosis → Asbestos fibers

  • Alkaptonuria → Homogentisic acid (ochronosis)

Pathology.question: ২৭) Apoptosis is
Pathology.exp:
Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, energy-dependent form of cell death that removes unwanted or damaged cells without causing inflammation. It occurs in both physiological (e.g., embryogenesis, hormone-dependent tissue involution) and pathological conditions (e.g., DNA damage, viral infections).

Rapid Recall

  • Apoptosis = Programmed cell death

  • Caspases are the key executioner enzymes.

  • No inflammation

  • Physiological + Pathological processes both involve apoptosis.

Pathology.question: ২৮) Traumatic fat necrosis occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Traumatic fat necrosis most commonly occurs in the breast following trauma or surgery. It results from injury to adipose tissue, leading to necrosis of fat cells, inflammation, and fibrosis. Clinically, it may present as a firm, painless breast lump that can mimic carcinoma.

High-Yield

Types of fat necrosis

  • Enzymatic fat necrosis → Acute pancreatitis (peripancreatic fat)

  • Traumatic fat necrosis → Breast, subcutaneous fa

Rapid Recall

  • Breast trauma → Traumatic fat necrosis

  • Pancreatitis → Enzymatic fat necrosis

  • Brain infarct → Liquefactive necrosis

  • Most other infarcts → Coagulative necrosis

Pathology.question: ২৯) Free radical activity is checked by
Pathology.exp:
Catalase is a major antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from reactive oxygen species (ROS) by converting hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) into water and oxygen.

Reaction:

  • 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

High-Yield

Major antioxidant defenses

  • Superoxide dismutase (SOD): O₂⁻ → H₂O₂

  • Catalase: H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂ ✔

  • Glutathione peroxidase: H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides → H₂O (uses glutathione)

Rapid Recall

  • NADPH oxidase → Produces ROS

  • SOD → Superoxide → H₂O₂

  • Catalase → H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂

  • Glutathione peroxidase → Detoxifies H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides

Pathology.question: ৩০) Not a Pathognomonic feature of VT
Pathology.exp:
In ventricular tachycardia (VT), the following ECG findings are considered highly specific/pathognomonic:

  • Capture beats ✔

  • Fusion beats ✔

  • Atrioventricular (AV) dissociation ✔

Extreme left axis deviation (northwest axis) strongly suggests VT, but it is not pathognomonic, as it can occur in other conditions.

High-Yield

Pathognomonic ECG features of VT

  • AV dissociation

  • Capture beats

  • Fusion beats

ECG features favoring VT

  • Broad QRS (>140–160 ms)

  • Extreme axis deviation ("northwest axis")

  • Concordance across precordial leads

  • Initial R wave in aVR

Rapid Recall

  • Capture beat = Diagnostic of VT

  • Fusion beat = Diagnostic of VT

  • AV dissociation = Diagnostic of VT

  • Extreme axis deviation = Suggests VT, but not pathognomonic

Pathology.question: ৩১) Which lung cancer is common in women?
Pathology.exp:
Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in women, especially in non-smokers. It usually arises peripherally in the lung and is the most common histological subtype overall.

Rapid Recall

  • Women + Non-smoker → Adenocarcinoma

  • Peripheral lung cancer → Adenocarcinoma

  • Central + Cavitation → Squamous cell carcinoma

  • Central + SIADH/ACTH → Small cell carcinoma

Pathology.question: ৩২) Lung cancers particularly related to paraneoplastic syndrome
Pathology.exp:
Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is the lung cancer most strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes because it is a neuroendocrine tumor capable of ectopic hormone production.

Common paraneoplastic syndromes in SCLC:

  • SIADH → Ectopic ADH

  • Cushing syndrome → Ectopic ACTH

  • Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome

  • Peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar degeneration

Rapid Recall

  • Small cell → SIADH + ACTH + Lambert–Eaton

  • Squamous → PTHrP → Hypercalcemia

  • Small cell = Most paraneoplastic syndromes

Pathology.question: ৩৩) Mechanism of heart failure following MI
Pathology.exp:
Following a myocardial infarction (MI), necrosis of cardiac muscle leads to loss of functioning myocardium, resulting in reduced left ventricular contractility. This decreases stroke volume and cardiac output, causing systolic heart failure.

High-Yield

Mechanisms of heart failure

  • MI → Reduced myocardial contractility → Systolic heart failure (HFrEF) ✔

  • Hypertension → Pressure overload

  • Mitral/Aortic regurgitation → Volume overload

  • Aortic stenosis → Outflow obstruction

  • Mitral stenosis → Inflow obstruction

Rapid Recall

  • MI → ↓ Contractility → ↓ Ejection fraction → HFrEF

  • Pressure overload → Concentric hypertrophy

  • Volume overload → Eccentric hypertrophy

  • Post-MI mechanical complications: Papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free-wall rupture

Pathology.question: ৩৪) The inflammatory cell in both acute & chronic viral hepatitis mainly
Pathology.exp:
In both acute and chronic viral hepatitis, the predominant inflammatory cells are T lymphocytes, especially CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells. These cells recognize viral antigens presented on infected hepatocytes and mediate immune-induced hepatocyte injury.

High-Yield

Predominant inflammatory cells

  • Acute viral hepatitis: CD8⁺ T lymphocytes

  • Chronic viral hepatitis: Mononuclear infiltrate predominantly T lymphocytes (portal tracts and interface hepatitis)

Rapid Recall

  • Viral hepatitis → T-cell-mediated liver injury

  • CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells → Hepatocyte apoptosis

  • Portal tract mononuclear infiltrate → Chronic hepatitis

  • Councilman bodies = Apoptotic hepatocytes

Pathology.question: ৩৫) Dystrophic calcification occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Dystrophic calcification is the deposition of calcium in dead or damaged tissues despite normal serum calcium levels. A classic example is caseous necrosis in a tuberculous lymph node, which frequently undergoes dystrophic calcification.

High-Yield

Dystrophic calcification (Normal serum Ca²⁺)

  • Tuberculous lymph node ✔

  • Atherosclerotic plaques

  • Damaged heart valves

  • Fat necrosis

  • Old infarcts

Metastatic calcification (High serum Ca²⁺)

  • Hyperparathyroidism

  • Vitamin D intoxication

  • Chronic kidney disease

  • Multiple myeloma

  • Sarcoidosis

Rapid Recall

  • Dead tissue + Normal Ca²⁺ → Dystrophic calcification

  • Hypercalcemia + Normal tissue → Metastatic calcification

  • TB lymph node → Dystrophic calcification

  • Sarcoidosis, Multiple myeloma → Metastatic calcification

Pathology.question: ৩৬) Metastatic calcification occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Metastatic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts in normal tissues due to hypercalcemia or disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism.

Paget disease of bone can be associated with hypercalcemia (especially during immobilization), predisposing to metastatic calcification.

High-Yield

Dystrophic calcification (Normal serum Ca²⁺)

  • Tuberculous lymph node

  • Caseous necrosis

  • Coagulative necrosis

  • Atherosclerotic plaques

  • Damaged heart valves

Metastatic calcification (Hypercalcemia)

  • Hyperparathyroidism

  • Vitamin D intoxication

  • Chronic kidney disease (secondary hyperparathyroidism)

  • Multiple myeloma

  • Paget disease (occasionally, especially with immobilization)

Rapid Recall

  • Necrotic tissue → Dystrophic calcification

  • Hypercalcemia → Metastatic calcification

  • TB lymph node → Dystrophic

  • Paget disease → Metastatic

Pathology.question: ৩৭) Endogenous pigment that accumulates inside the cell is
Pathology.exp:
Lipofuscin is an endogenous intracellular pigment formed by lipid peroxidation of cellular membranes. It is known as the "wear-and-tear" pigment and accumulates in aging cells, particularly in the heart, liver, and neurons.

High-Yield

Endogenous pigments

  • Lipofuscin – Wear-and-tear pigment

  • Melanin – Brown-black pigment

  • Hemosiderin – Iron-storage pigment

  • Bilirubin – Bile pigment

Exogenous pigments

  • Carbon dust

  • Coal dust

  • Tattoo pigment

Rapid Recall

  • Lipofuscin = Aging (wear-and-tear) pigment

  • Hemosiderin = Iron

  • Melanin = Skin pigmentation

  • Carbon/Coal dust = Exogenous pigment

Pathology.question: ৩৮) Hypertrophy usually occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells, not the number of cells. It occurs mainly in non-dividing (permanent) cells, which cannot undergo mitosis in response to increased workload.

Typical examples include:

  • Cardiac muscle (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis)

  • Skeletal muscle (e.g., exercise)

Examples of hypertrophy

  • Left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension

  • Skeletal muscle hypertrophy with exercise

  • Pregnant uterus → Both hypertrophy and hyperplasia

Rapid Recall

  • Hypertrophy = ↑ Cell size

  • Hyperplasia = ↑ Cell number

  • Cardiac muscle → Hypertrophy only

  • Labile cells → Hyperplasia

  • Pregnant uterus → Both hypertrophy + hyperplasia

Pathology.question: ৩৯) Generalized atrophy occurs in
Pathology.exp:
Generalized atrophy affects the entire body or multiple organs. Senile atrophy is a physiological generalized atrophy that occurs with aging, affecting organs such as the brain, heart, skeletal muscles, and gonads.

High-Yield

Generalized atrophy

  • Senile (aging) ✔

  • Starvation/cachexia

  • Cancer cachexia

Localized atrophy

  • Disuse

  • Denervation

  • Ischemia

  • Loss of endocrine stimulation

  • Pressure

Rapid Recall

  • Aging → Generalized atrophy

  • Disuse → Localized muscle atrophy

  • Pressure → Localized atrophy

  • Loss of hormones → Endometrium/Breast atrophy

Pathology.question: ৪০) Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in
Pathology.exp:
Fibrinoid necrosis is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes and fibrin in the walls of blood vessels. It is classically seen in immune-mediated vasculitis and malignant hypertension.

Rapid Recall

  • SLE → Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Brain infarct → Liquefactive necrosis

  • TB → Caseous necrosis

  • Boil → Liquefactive necrosis

Pathology.question: ৪১) Ground glass cells are found in chronic infection with hepatitis
৪২) Gastric metastasis to pouch of Doglas is known as
Pathology.exp:
Blumer shelf is a metastatic deposit in the rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas) or rectovesical pouch, classically from gastric carcinoma. On digital rectal examination, it is felt as a hard shelf-like mass.

Rapid Recall

  • Virchow → Left supraclavicular

  • Irish → Left axillary

  • Blumer shelf → Pouch of Douglas

  • Sister Mary Joseph → Umbilicus

Pathology.question: ৪৩) A patient came to you with features of impaired wound healing. The patient is undernourished. Which vitamins may be may be related with this-
Pathology.option4: Vit B12, Vit C, Vit D
Pathology.exp:
Several vitamin deficiencies can impair wound healing, but the most important are Vitamin C and Vitamin A. Vitamin D also contributes by modulating immunity and tissue repair. Among the given options, Vitamin A + Vitamin C + Vitamin D is the best answer.

High-Yield

Vitamins important for wound healing

  • Vitamin C → Collagen synthesis (hydroxylation of proline and lysine)

  • Vitamin A → Epithelial regeneration, fibroblast function, immune response

  • Vitamin D → Immune modulation and tissue repair

  • Vitamin K → Hemostasis (not tissue repair)

  • Vitamin B complex → General metabolism, not primary wound-healing vitamins

Rapid Recall

  • Vitamin C deficiency → Poor collagen → Poor wound healing

  • Vitamin A → Epithelial repair

  • Zinc is also essential for wound healing (common MCQ point)

  • Undernutrition + poor wound healing → Think Protein, Vitamin C, Vitamin A, Zinc

Pathology.question: ৪৪) Which of the following types of necrosis is most characteristic of abscess formation?
Pathology.exp:
An abscess is caused by pyogenic bacterial infection, leading to the accumulation of neutrophils. These cells release hydrolytic enzymes that digest dead tissue, resulting in liquefactive necrosis and the formation of pus.

High-Yield

Type of necrosis Classic example
Coagulative Myocardial infarction, renal infarction
Liquefactive Abscess, brain infarction
Caseous Tuberculosis
Fat (enzymatic) Acute pancreatitis
Fibrinoid SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, malignant hypertension

Rapid Recall

  • Abscess → Liquefactive necrosis

  • Brain infarct → Liquefactive necrosis

  • TB → Caseous necrosis

  • MI → Coagulative necrosis

Pathology.question: ৪৫) A 25-year-old man has a lifelong hemorrhagic diathesis. The PT and bleeding time are normal, but the APTT is prolonged. The most likely cause of the bleeding disorder is
Pathology.exp:
The patient has:

  • Lifelong hemorrhagic diathesis → Suggests a congenital coagulation disorder.

  • Normal PT → Extrinsic pathway is intact.

  • Normal bleeding time (BT) → Platelet function is normal.

  • Prolonged APTT → Defect in the intrinsic pathway (Factors VIII, IX, XI, XII).

The most common inherited intrinsic pathway defect is Factor VIII deficiency (Hemophilia A).

Rapid Recall

  • Hemophilia A = Factor VIII deficiency

  • Hemophilia B = Factor IX deficiency

  • Intrinsic pathway → APTT ↑

  • Extrinsic pathway → PT ↑

  • vWD → Bleeding time ↑

Pathology.question: ৪৬) Pseudomembranous enterocolitis is caused by-
Pathology.exp:
Pseudomembranous enterocolitis (pseudomembranous colitis) is caused by Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile), usually following broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (e.g., clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin).

The organism produces:

  • Toxin A (enterotoxin)

  • Toxin B (cytotoxin) – the major virulence factor causing mucosal injury and pseudomembrane formation.

High-Yield

  • Cause: Clostridioides difficile

  • Risk factor: Recent antibiotic use

  • Diagnosis: Stool test for toxins A/B or NAAT (PCR)

  • Colonoscopy: Yellow-white pseudomembranes

  • Treatment:

    • First-line: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin

    • Stop the offending antibiotic if possible

Rapid Recall

  • Pseudomembranous colitis → C. difficile

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics → Major risk factor

  • Toxins A & B → Colonic mucosal damage

  • Treatment → Oral vancomycin or fidaxomici

Pathology.question: ৪৭) Non-Specific antibody tests for syphilis are
Pathology.exp:
VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) is a non-treponemal (non-specific) test for syphilis. It detects reagin antibodies directed against cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen, not antibodies against Treponema pallidum itself.

High-Yield

Non-treponemal (Screening) tests

  • VDRL

  • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin)

Treponemal (Confirmatory) tests

  • TPHA

  • TPPA

  • FTA-ABS

  • EIA/CIA for T. pallidum

Rapid Recall

  • VDRL, RPR → Screening, non-specific, titers used for monitoring treatment

  • TPHA, TPPA, FTA-ABS → Confirmatory, specific, usually remain positive for life

Pathology.question: ৪৮) Chronic carrier state of typhoid fever lies in
৪৯) Shape of Vibrio cholera
৫০) Which one remains positive for life in syphilis?
৫১) Amastigote form of leishmania donovani are detected in:
Pathology.exp:
Leishmania donovani exists in two forms:

  • Amastigote (Leishman-Donovan bodies): Found inside macrophages in humans, especially in the bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, and liver.

  • Promastigote: Found in the infected female sandfly.

Bone marrow aspiration is a common and relatively safe method for demonstrating amastigotes (LD bodies) in patients with visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

High-Yield

  • Human infective stage: Promastigote

  • Human tissue stage: Amastigote (LD bodies)

  • Diagnostic specimens: Bone marrow aspirate, splenic aspirate (most sensitive), lymph node aspirate

  • Vector: Female Phlebotomus sandfly

Rapid Recall

  • Sandfly → Promastigote

  • Human macrophages → Amastigote (LD bodies)

  • Diagnosis → Bone marrow aspirate

Pathology.question: ৫২) Why anaemia occurs in kala azar?
Pathology.exp:
Anaemia in visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is multifactorial, but the single best answer is hypersplenism. Massive splenomegaly leads to sequestration and increased destruction of red blood cells, contributing to pancytopenia.

Other contributing factors include:

  • Bone marrow suppression/infiltration by infected macrophages

  • Chronic inflammation (anaemia of chronic disease)

  • Nutritional deficiencies

High-Yield

  • Kala-azar → Massive splenomegaly → Hypersplenism

  • Pancytopenia: Anaemia + Leukopenia + Thrombocytopenia

  • Amastigotes (LD bodies): Found in macrophages of bone marrow, spleen, and liver

Rapid Recall

  • Most common cause of anaemia in kala-azar → Hypersplenism

  • Massive splenomegaly → Pancytopenia

  • Bone marrow aspirate → Demonstrates LD bodies

Pathology.question: ৫৩) Thick or Thin film are used in diagnosis of:
Pathology.exp:
Thick and thin peripheral blood films are the gold standard microscopic tests for diagnosing malaria.

  • Thick blood film: More sensitive; used to detect malaria parasites, especially when parasitemia is low.

  • Thin blood film: Used to identify the Plasmodium species and estimate the parasite density (parasitemia).

High-Yield

  • Thick smear: Detects parasites (highest sensitivity).

  • Thin smear: Identifies Plasmodium species and quantifies parasitemia.

  • Gold standard microscopy: Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films.

Rapid Recall

  • Thick film → Detection

  • Thin film → Species identification

  • Malaria diagnosis → Thick + Thin peripheral blood smear

Pathology.question: ৫৪) Which of the following nematodes pass via lung during their life cycle:
Pathology.exp:
Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) larvae penetrate the skin, enter the bloodstream, migrate to the lungs, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and finally mature in the small intestine. This heart–lung migration is a characteristic feature of hookworms.

High-Yield

Nematodes with lung migration:

  • ✔ Ancylostoma duodenale

  • ✔ Necator americanus

  • ✔ Ascaris lumbricoides

  • ✔ Strongyloides stercoralis

Nematodes without lung migration:

  • ✘ Trichuris trichiura

  • ✘ Enterobius vermicularis

  • ✘ Brugia malayi

  • ✘ Wuchereria bancrofti

Rapid Recall

  • Hookworm (A. duodenale) → Skin → Blood → Lung → Trachea → Gut

  • Ascaris and Strongyloides also undergo lung migration.

  • FCPS tip: If hookworm is among the options, it is usually the best answer for lung migration.

Pathology.question: ৫৫) Which is the most significant risk factor for COPD
Pathology.exp:
Cigarette smoking is mo

Cigarette smoking is the most significant and common risk factor for COPD worldwide. Approximately 80–90% of COPD cases in high-income countries are attributable to cigarette smoking. It causes chronic airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and destruction of alveolar walls (emphysema).

High-Yield

  • Most important risk factor: Cigarette smoking

  • Most important genetic risk factor: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

  • Other risk factors:

    • Biomass fuel/indoor air pollution

    • Occupational dusts and chemicals

    • Outdoor air pollution

    • Recurrent respiratory infections

Rapid Recall

  • COPD → Cigarette smoking

  • Young non-smoker with emphysema → Think α1-antitrypsin deficiency

  • Biomass fuel exposure → Important COPD risk factor in developing countries

st common risk factor in COPD

Pathology.question: ৫৬) Right-to-left shunts are most commonly caused by
Pathology.exp:
A right-to-left shunt occurs when deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the systemic circulation, causing cyanosis. The most common congenital cyanotic heart disease beyond the neonatal period and the classic cause of a right-to-left shunt is Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

High-Yield

Left-to-Right Shunts (Acyanotic)

  • ASD

  • VSD (most common congenital heart defect)

  • PDA

Right-to-Left Shunts (Cyanotic)

  • Tetralogy of Fallot (most common)

  • Transposition of the great arteries

  • Tricuspid atresia

  • Truncus arteriosus

  • Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (obstructed)

Rapid Recall

  • TOF → Right-to-left shunt → Cyanosis

  • ASD, VSD, PDA → Left-to-right shunts

  • Long-standing left-to-right shunt → Eisenmenger syndrome → Right-to-left shunt reversal

Pathology.question: ৫৭) Secondary TB mostly occurs due to
Pathology.exp:
Secondary (post-primary/reactivation) tuberculosis usually results from reactivation of latent infection when cell-mediated immunity is impaired. Among the given options, AIDS (HIV infection) is the strongest and most important risk factor because it causes profound CD4⁺ T-cell depletion, markedly increasing the risk of TB reactivation.

High-Yield

  • Primary TB: Usually in previously unexposed children or young adults.

  • Secondary TB: Reactivation due to immunosuppression, especially HIV/AIDS.

  • Common site: Apical (upper lobe) of the lung.

  • Risk factors: HIV/AIDS, corticosteroids, TNF-α inhibitors, diabetes mellitus, CKD, malnutrition.

Rapid Recall

  • Primary TB → Initial infection

  • Secondary TB → Reactivation

  • Strongest risk factor → HIV/AIDS

  • Site of secondary TB → Upper lobe (apex)

Pathology.question: ৫৮) Most important modifiable risk factor of coronary artery disease(CAD)
Pathology.exp:
Among the modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease (CAD), cigarette smoking is considered the most important because it accelerates atherosclerosis, promotes thrombosis, causes endothelial dysfunction, and increases the risk of myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death.

High-Yield

Non-modifiable risk factors

  • Increasing age

  • Male sex

  • Family history of premature CAD

Modifiable risk factors

  • Smoking (most important)

  • Dyslipidaemia (especially ↑LDL)

  • Hypertension

  • Diabetes mellitus

  • Obesity

  • Physical inactivity

Rapid Recall

  • Most important modifiable risk factor for CAD → Smoking

  • Most important lipid abnormality → Elevated LDL cholesterol

  • Diabetes mellitus → CAD risk equivalent

  • Smoking cessation reduces CAD risk substantially

Pathology.question: ৫৯) Most common primary cardiac tumour in adults
Pathology.exp:
Cardiac myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. It is a benign tumor, with about 75% arising in the left atrium, usually attached to the interatrial septum (fossa ovalis) by a stalk.

High-Yield

  • Most common primary cardiac tumor (adults): Myxoma

  • Most common primary cardiac tumor (children): Rhabdomyoma

  • Most common primary malignant cardiac tumor: Angiosarcoma

  • Most common site of myxoma: Left atrium

Rapid Recall

  • Adult → Myxoma

  • Child → Rhabdomyoma

  • Left atrium + constitutional symptoms + embolism → Think myxoma

  • Malignant primary cardiac tumor → Angiosarcoma

Pathology.question: ৬০) Pathognomonic for acute rheumatic fever
Pathology.exp:
Aschoff nodules (Aschoff bodies) are the pathognomonic histological lesion of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). They are granulomatous lesions composed of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and activated macrophages (Anitschkow "caterpillar" cells).

High-Yield

  • Pathognomonic lesion: Aschoff bodies

  • Characteristic cardiac involvement: Pancarditis (endocarditis + myocarditis + pericarditis)

  • Characteristic cell: Anitschkow (caterpillar) cell

  • Pericarditis: Classically causes "bread-and-butter" fibrinous pericarditis

Rapid Recall

  • Acute rheumatic fever → Aschoff bodies

  • Pancarditis → Characteristic cardiac lesion

  • Anitschkow cells → Caterpillar nuclei

  • Jones criteria → Diagnose ARF

Pathology.question: ৬১) Swarming growth in blood agar media found for-
Pathology.exp:
Proteus species (especially Proteus mirabilis) characteristically produce swarming growth on blood agar, appearing as concentric waves due to their highly motile peritrichous flagella.

High-Yield

  • Swarming growth: Proteus spp.

  • Urease: Strongly positive

  • H₂S production: Positive

  • Associated with: UTIs, struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate)

Rapid Recall

  • Proteus → Swarming on blood agar

  • Proteus → Urease positive

  • Proteus → H₂S positive

  • Proteus → Struvite (staghorn) calculi

Pathology.question: ৬২) Most common cause of nosocomial diarrhoea-
Pathology.exp:
Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile is the most common cause of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) diarrhea. It usually occurs after broad-spectrum antibiotic use, which disrupts the normal intestinal flora, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile. Its toxins A and B cause pseudomembranous colitis.

High-Yield

  • Most common cause of nosocomial diarrhea: Clostridioides difficile

  • Risk factors: Recent antibiotics (especially clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), hospitalization, advanced age, PPI use.

  • Diagnosis: Stool test for C. difficile toxin or NAAT (PCR).

  • Treatment (initial episode): Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.

Rapid Recall

  • Nosocomial diarrhea → C. difficile

  • Pseudomembranous colitis → C. difficile

  • Toxins → A (enterotoxin) & B (cytotoxin)

  • Classic risk factor → Recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use

Pathology.question: ৬৩) Main agent in necrotizing fasciitis-
Pathology.exp:
The most common causative organism of necrotizing fasciitis is Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) (Type II necrotizing fasciitis). It spreads rapidly along the fascial planes, causing extensive tissue necrosis and systemic toxicity.

High-Yield

  • Most common organism: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes)

  • Type I necrotizing fasciitis: Polymicrobial (anaerobes + Enterobacterales + streptococci)

  • Type II necrotizing fasciitis: Monomicrobial, usually Group A Streptococcus

  • Treatment: Urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + vancomycin)

Rapid Recall

  • Necrotizing fasciitis → Group A Streptococcus

  • Rapid progression + severe pain out of proportion

  • Management → Emergency surgery + IV antibiotics

  • Clindamycin → Suppresses streptococcal toxin production

Pathology.question: ৬৪) Which chemical structure is septic shock inducer?
Pathology.exp:
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is the endotoxin present in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. Its Lipid A component triggers massive release of TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6, leading to systemic inflammatory response, vasodilation, hypotension, DIC, and ultimately septic shock.

High-Yield

  • Endotoxin: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)

  • Toxic component: Lipid A

  • Found in: Gram-negative bacteria

  • Cytokines released: TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6

  • Clinical effects: Fever, hypotension, DIC, septic shock

Rapid Recall

  • Gram-negative endotoxin → LPS

  • Active toxic portion → Lipid A

  • Exotoxin → Protein

  • Endotoxin → Heat stable; Exotoxin → Usually heat labile

Pathology.question: ৬৫) Site of infection for Campylobacter jejuni
৬৬) Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by
৬৭) Chronic bronchitis is defined as persistent productive cough for at least …consecutive months in at least 2 consecutive years?
Pathology.exp:
Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined as a persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, provided that other causes of chronic cough have been excluded.

High-Yield

  • Definition: Productive cough for ≥3 months/year for ≥2 consecutive years

  • Major cause: Cigarette smoking

  • Pathology: Mucous gland hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia

  • Reid index: >0.5 (hallmark pathological finding)

Rapid Recall

  • 3 months + 2 years = Chronic bronchitis

  • Reid index >0.5

  • "Blue bloater" phenotype

  • Part of COPD

Pathology.question: ৬৮) Features of right heart failure excludes
Pathology.exp:
The clinical features of right heart failure are mainly due to systemic venous congestion.

Typical findings include:

  • Raised JVP

  • Hepatomegaly

  • Peripheral edema

  • Ascites

Cardiomegaly is a radiological finding, not a characteristic clinical feature of right heart failure. It may be present depending on the underlying heart disease but is not a defining feature of right-sided heart failure.

High-Yield

Right heart failure features:

  • Raised JVP

  • Peripheral edema

  • Hepatomegaly

  • Ascites

  • Hepatojugular reflux

Rapid Recall

  • Right HF → Systemic venous congestion

  • Raised JVP + Hepatomegaly + Ascites + Pedal edema

  • Cardiomegaly → X-ray finding, not a clinical feature

Pathology.question: ৬৯) Most important risk factor for chronic bronchitis
Pathology.exp:
Cigarette smoking is the most important risk factor for chronic bronchitis. It causes chronic airway inflammation, goblet cell hyperplasia, mucous gland hypertrophy, and impaired mucociliary clearance, leading to chronic productive cough.

High-Yield

  • Most important risk factor: Cigarette smoking

  • Definition: Productive cough for ≥3 months/year in ≥2 consecutive years

  • Pathological hallmark: Reid index >0.5

  • Part of: COPD

Rapid Recall

  • Chronic bronchitis → Smoking

  • Reid index >0.5

  • "Blue bloater" phenotype

  • Most important preventive measure → Smoking cessation

Pathology.question: ৭০) Most common congenital cardiac malformation
Pathology.exp:
Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease at birth. It accounts for approximately 20–30% of all congenital cardiac malformations. Small VSDs may close spontaneously, while large defects can lead to left-to-right shunt, pulmonary hypertension, and eventually Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated.

High-Yield

  • Most common congenital heart disease: VSD

  • Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) (after the neonatal period)

  • Most common cyanotic CHD in newborns: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)

  • Most common congenital cardiac malformation in adults: Bicuspid aortic valve (often excluded in pediatric MCQs)

Rapid Recall

  • Most common CHD → VSD

  • Most common cyanotic CHD → TOF

  • Most common cyanotic CHD in neonates → TGA

  • Most common adult congenital valve lesion → Bicuspid aortic valve

Pathology.question: ৭১) Kaposi’s sarcoma is caused by
৭২) Predisposing factor for toxic shock syndrome
৭৩) Endocarditis on prosthetic heart valve is caused by
Pathology.exp:
Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) is classically caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. It forms biofilms on prosthetic material, making it the most common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis.

High-Yield

  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis → S. epidermidis

  • Native valve endocarditis (acute) → S. aureus

  • Subacute native valve endocarditis → Viridans streptococci

  • IV drug users → S. aureus (often tricuspid valve)

Rapid Recall

  • Prosthetic valve → S. epidermidis

  • Coagulase-negative

  • Biofilm producer

  • Novobiocin sensitive (S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant)

Pathology.question: ৭৪) Line of zahn are marked in thrombi formed within
Pathology.exp:
Lines of Zahn are alternating pale platelet-fibrin layers and dark red blood cell-rich layers seen in thrombi formed in flowing blood before death (antemortem thrombi). They are most prominent in arteries, where blood flow is rapid, especially in the aorta.

Although Lines of Zahn can be present in the heart and large arteries (and may be less distinct in veins), the best single answer among the given options is aorta.

High-Yield

  • Lines of Zahn = Antemortem thrombus

  • Most prominent in arteries (especially the aorta) and cardiac chambers

  • Absent in postmortem clots

  • Composition: Alternating platelet-fibrin (pale) and RBC (dark) layers

Rapid Recall

  • Lines of Zahn → Antemortem thrombus

  • Best site → Aorta / large arteries

  • Postmortem clot → No Lines of Zahn

  • Venous thrombus → Red (RBC-rich) thrombus

Pathology.question: ৭৫) Accumulation of excess fluid in tissue is called
Pathology.exp:
Edema is the abnormal accumulation of excess fluid in the interstitial tissue spaces (and sometimes in body cavities). It results from disturbances in hydrostatic pressure, oncotic pressure, capillary permeability, or lymphatic drainage.

High-Yield

Causes of edema:

  • ↑ Hydrostatic pressure (e.g., heart failure)

  • ↓ Plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, liver disease)

  • ↑ Capillary permeability (e.g., inflammation)

  • Lymphatic obstruction (e.g., filariasis, malignancy)

  • Sodium and water retention

Rapid Recall

  • Edema → Excess interstitial fluid

  • Congestion → Passive venous blood accumulation

  • Hyperaemia → Active arteriolar dilatation

  • Shock → Inadequate tissue perfusion

Pathology.question: ৭৬) Exuberant scars that recur after excision are called
Pathology.exp:
An exuberant scar that extends beyond the original wound margins and frequently recurs after surgical excision is called a keloid.

A hypertrophic scar is raised but:

  • Remains confined to the original wound.

  • May regress over time.

  • Has a much lower recurrence rate after excision than a keloid.

Rapid Recall

  • Keloid → Extends beyond wound + Recurs after excision

  • Hypertrophic scar → Confined to wound + May regress

Note: If this is from an exam, it is likely a misprinted question. The intended answer is Keloid.

Pathology.question: ৭৭) Granulation tissue easily bleeds on touch due to rupture of
Pathology.exp:
Granulation tissue is composed of newly formed capillaries, proliferating fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells. The new capillaries are thin-walled, fragile, and immature, so they rupture easily, causing granulation tissue to bleed on touch.

High-Yield

Components of granulation tissue:

  • New capillaries (angiogenesis)

  • Fibroblasts

  • Loose extracellular matrix

  • Inflammatory cells (especially macrophages)

Clinical features:

  • Pink/red appearance

  • Soft and granular

  • Bleeds easily on touch

Rapid Recall

  • Granulation tissue → New capillaries + Fibroblasts

  • Bleeds easily → Fragile new capillaries

  • Macrophages → Key regulators of wound healing

Pathology.question: ৭৮) The process of coating a particle to target it for ingestion is called
Pathology.exp:
Opsonization is the process by which microorganisms or other particles are coated with opsonins, making them easier for phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages) to recognize and ingest.

The principal opsonins are:

  • IgG

  • C3b (complement)

  • Collectins (e.g., mannose-binding lectin)

High-Yield

Steps of leukocyte recruitment:

  1. Margination

  2. Rolling

  3. Adhesion

  4. Transmigration (Diapedesis)

  5. Chemotaxis

  6. Phagocytosis (enhanced by opsonization)

Rapid Recall

  • Opsonization → Coating for phagocytosis

  • IgG, C3b → Major opsonins

  • Chemotaxis → Leukocyte movement

  • Phagocytosis → Engulfment of pathogen

Pathology.question: ৭৯) UTI in young women is mostly caused by
৮০) Which streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis & meningitis?
৮১) Which organism causes endocarditis following dental procedure?
৮২) Dominant leukocyte in pus is
Pathology.exp:
Pus is a purulent exudate composed predominantly of neutrophils, along with necrotic tissue debris, microorganisms, and protein-rich inflammatory fluid. Neutrophils are the first responders in acute bacterial infections, making them the dominant leukocyte in pus.

High-Yield

  • Acute bacterial infection → Neutrophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Macrophages, lymphocytes

  • Parasitic infection/allergy → Eosinophils

  • Viral infection → Lymphocytes

Rapid Recall

  • Pus → Neutrophils

  • Acute inflammation → Neutrophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Macrophages

  • Allergy & parasites → Eosinophils

Pathology.question: ৮৩) Complement acting as opsonin is
Pathology.exp:
C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microorganisms, enhancing their recognition and phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages through complement receptors (CR1).

High-Yield

Complement Component Function
C3b Opsonization
C3a, C5a Anaphylatoxins
C5a Powerful chemotaxis for neutrophils
C5b–C9 Membrane attack complex (MAC)

Rapid Recall

  • C3b → Opsonization

  • C5a → Chemotaxis + Anaphylatoxin

  • C3a → Anaphylatoxin

  • C5b–C9 → Cell lysis (MAC)

Pathology.question: ৮৪) Complement products are produced in
Pathology.exp:
The liver is the principal site of synthesis of complement proteins (e.g., C1–C9). These proteins circulate in plasma as inactive precursors and are activated during the complement cascade.

High-Yield

  • Site of synthesis: Liver (hepatocytes)

  • Major complement functions:

    • C3b → Opsonization

    • C3a, C5a → Anaphylatoxins

    • C5a → Chemotaxis

    • C5b–C9 → Membrane attack complex (MAC)

Rapid Recall

  • Complement proteins → Liver

  • C3b → Opsonization

  • C5a → Chemotaxis

  • C5b–C9 → MAC (cell lysis)

Pathology.question: ৮৫) Arachidonic acid derived mediators are called
Pathology.exp:
Arachidonic acid is metabolized by the cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX) pathways to produce eicosanoids, which are important inflammatory mediators.

Eicosanoids include:

  • Prostaglandins (PGs)

  • Thromboxanes (TXA₂)

  • Leukotrienes (LTs)

  • Lipoxins

High-Yield

Arachidonic acid pathway:

  • COX → Prostaglandins, Thromboxanes

  • 5-LOX → Leukotrienes

  • 12/15-LOX → Lipoxins

Rapid Recall

  • Arachidonic acid → Eicosanoids

  • COX → PGs, TXA₂

  • LOX → LTs, Lipoxins

  • NSAIDs inhibit COX

Pathology.question: ৮৬) Main source of TNF is
Pathology.exp:
Macrophages (activated tissue macrophages/monocytes) are the principal source of Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF-α) during inflammation. TNF-α is a key pro-inflammatory cytokine that mediates fever, endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, cachexia, and septic shock.

Rapid Recall

  • TNF-α → Macrophages

  • IL-1 → Fever

  • IL-6 → CRP production

  • TNF-α + IL-1 → Endothelial activation & septic shock

Pathology.question: ৮৭) Dominant cellular player in chronic inflammation is
Pathology.exp:
Macrophages are the dominant cellular players in chronic inflammation. They are activated by cytokines (especially IFN-γ from T lymphocytes) and secrete inflammatory mediators, growth factors, and enzymes that are responsible for persistent inflammation, tissue destruction, and fibrosis.

High-Yield

Cells in Chronic Inflammation:

  • Macrophages → Dominant cell

  • Lymphocytes → Regulate immune response

  • Plasma cells → Antibody production

  • Fibroblasts → Fibrosis and tissue repair

Rapid Recall

  • Acute inflammation → Neutrophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Macrophages

  • Allergy/Parasites → Eosinophils

  • Immediate hypersensitivity → Mast cells

Pathology.question: ৮৮) Spores germinate in reheated rice
৮৯) Causes of chronic type-2 respiratory failure excludes
Pathology.exp:
Type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is characterized by:

  • PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (8 kPa)

  • PaCO₂ > 50 mmHg (6.7 kPa)

Chronic Type 2 respiratory failure develops due to chronic alveolar hypoventilation.

High-Yield

Causes of Chronic Type 2 Respiratory Failure:

  • COPD

  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

  • Obstructive sleep apnoea

  • Neuromuscular disorders (e.g., myopathies, MND, muscular dystrophy)

  • Chest wall deformities (e.g., kyphoscoliosis)

Rapid Recall

  • Type 1: ↓PaO₂, normal/↓PaCO₂ → Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, lobar collapse, PE

  • Type 2: ↓PaO₂, ↑PaCO₂ → COPD, OSA/OHS, neuromuscular disease, chest wall disorders

Pathology.question: ৯০) Rheumatic heart disease most commonly affects
Pathology.exp:
Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) most commonly affects the mitral valve due to autoimmune inflammation following Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcal pharyngitis.

Valve involvement (most to least common):

  1. Mitral valve (most common)

  2. Mitral + Aortic valves

  3. Aortic valve alone

  4. Tricuspid valve

  5. Pulmonary valve (rare)

In chronic RHD, the most common lesion is mitral stenosis.

High-Yield

  • Most commonly affected valve: Mitral

  • Most common chronic lesion: Mitral stenosis

  • Most common acute lesion: Mitral regurgitation

  • Organism: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus)

Rapid Recall

  • RHD → Mitral valve

  • Mitral stenosis → Most common chronic RHD lesion

  • Mitral + Aortic → Most common combined involvement

  • Pulmonary valve → Rarely affected

Pathology.question: ৯১) Most common form of cardiomyopathy
Pathology.exp:
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common form of cardiomyopathy. It is characterized by dilatation of one or both ventricles with impaired systolic function (reduced ejection fraction).

Rapid Recall

  • Most common cardiomyopathy → Dilated

  • Most common inherited cardiomyopathy → Hypertrophic

  • Restrictive → Amyloidosis, hemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis

  • Constrictive ≠ Cardiomyopathy (Pericardial disease)

Pathology.question: ৯২) Which clostridium causes gas gangrene?
৯৩) Dysentery is caused by
৯৪) The obligate intracellular bacteria –
Pathology.exp:
Rickettsia prowazekii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium. It can only survive and replicate within living host cells, particularly endothelial cells, and causes epidemic typhus.

High-Yield

Obligate intracellular bacteria:

  • Rickettsia spp.

  • Chlamydia spp.

  • Coxiella burnetii (also intracellular)

Rapid Recall

  • Rickettsia → Epidemic typhus → Obligate intracellular

  • Chlamydia → Obligate intracellular

  • Legionella → Facultative intracellular

  • Mycoplasma → No cell wall

Pathology.question: ৯৫) Non capsular Organisms -
Pathology.exp:
Cryptosporidium spp. are protozoan parasites and do not possess a bacterial capsule. In contrast, the other three organisms are well-known encapsulated pathogens.

High-Yield

Important Encapsulated Organisms (Remember: "SHiNE SKiS")

  • S – Streptococcus pneumoniae

  • H – Haemophilus influenzae type b

  • N – Neisseria meningitidis

  • E – Escherichia coli (K1)

  • S – Salmonella (Vi antigen)

  • K – Klebsiella pneumoniae

  • iS – Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)

Rapid Recall

  • Non-capsular → Cryptosporidium spp.

  • Hib → Capsule (PRP)

  • Pneumococcus → Capsule

  • Klebsiella → Thick capsule

Pathology.question: ৯৬) Diseases caused by viridans streptococcus
Pathology.exp:
Viridans streptococci are α-hemolytic streptococci that are part of the normal oral flora. They commonly cause subacute infective endocarditis, particularly in patients with previously damaged or abnormal heart valves, often following dental procedures.

Rapid Recall

  • Viridans streptococci → Subacute infective endocarditis

  • Dental procedure → Viridans streptococci

  • Prosthetic valve → S. epidermidis

  • IV drug user → S. aureus

Pathology.question: ৯৭) Hallmark of SLE
Pathology.exp:
The hallmark of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is the production of autoantibodies against nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens, leading to the formation of immune complexes and multisystem inflammation.

Although female predominance, arthritis, and skin rash (malar rash) are common features, they are not the defining hallmark of the disease.

High-Yield

  • Hallmark: Autoantibody production

  • Screening test: ANA (high sensitivity)

  • Highly specific antibodies: Anti-dsDNA, Anti-Sm

  • Pathogenesis: Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex-mediated)

Rapid Recall

  • Hallmark of SLE → Autoantibodies

  • Most sensitive test → ANA

  • Most specific tests → Anti-dsDNA, Anti-Sm

  • Low C3/C4 → Active SLE

Pathology.question: ৯৮) Most common cause of bronchiactesis
Pathology.exp:
Bronchiectasis is permanent dilatation of the bronchi caused by chronic infection and inflammation. Post-infectious bronchiectasis, especially following severe suppurative (necrotizing) pneumonia, is the most common acquired cause worldwide and is the best answer among the given options.

High-Yield

  • Most common acquired cause: Post-infectious (suppurative pneumonia)

  • Most common inherited cause: Cystic fibrosis

  • Other causes: Tuberculosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, bronchial obstruction, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).

Rapid Recall

  • Bronchiectasis → Suppurative pneumonia (acquired)

  • Inherited bronchiectasis → Cystic fibrosis

  • Localized bronchiectasis → Bronchial obstruction/tumor

  • TB → Important cause in high-prevalence countries

Pathology.question: ৯৯) Key inflammatory cell in asthma
Pathology.exp:
Eosinophils are the key inflammatory cells in bronchial asthma, particularly allergic (atopic) asthma. They are recruited by IL-5 released from Th2 lymphocytes and release major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein, and leukotrienes, leading to airway inflammation, epithelial damage, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.

High-Yield

  • Key inflammatory cell: Eosinophil

  • Key cytokine: IL-5

  • IgE production: IL-4, IL-13

  • Immediate mediator: Mast cells (histamine, leukotrienes)

Rapid Recall

  • Asthma → Eosinophils

  • COPD → Neutrophils, macrophages

  • IL-5 → Eosinophil activation

  • Major Basic Protein (MBP) → Airway epithelial damage

Pathology.question: ১০০) Which of the following is a toxin-mediated disease caused by Staphylococcus aureus?
Pathology.exp:
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a toxin-mediated disease caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen that causes massive cytokine release.

High-Yield

Toxin-mediated diseases of Staphylococcus aureus:

  • Toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1)

  • Scalded skin syndrome (Exfoliative toxins A & B)

  • Food poisoning/Gastroenteritis (Preformed enterotoxin)

Rapid Recall

  • TSST-1 → Toxic shock syndrome → S. aureus

  • Exfoliative toxin → Scalded skin syndrome

  • Enterotoxin → Food poisoning

  • Scarlet fever, ARF, PSGN → Streptococcus pyogenes
